lines: Here's a value nobody thinks to worry about: somebody's own name.

A customer named Smith, comma, John lands in an export exactly where a column boundary could be, and a reader that just splits on every comma it sees counts four columns where there are really only three.
The reader isn't broken. It's doing exactly what it was told to do, split on every comma, and that instruction turns out to be the wrong one.
Quoting that field fixed the comma, so it's tempting to think quoting just solves everything that could trip up a reader.
Here's a second field, this time with a quote mark living inside it.
Does wrapping it in quotes handle that too, or does an embedded quote need some rule all its own?
answer: Quoting really did solve the comma, and that's exactly what makes this tempting.
But quoting only tells a reader where a field starts and ends. It says nothing about a quote mark that shows up inside the field itself.
That's a second, completely separate rule, and it's what we look at next.

lines: If you've written code in almost any other language, your instinct here is a backslash, escape the quote the way you would in a string literal.
Try that in a plain text table and watch what a correct reader actually does with it: it reads back wrong, because a backslash means nothing special to this format at all.
The one rule this format actually has looks stranger but is far simpler: write the quote twice in a row, and that's the whole escape mechanism.
Every line based tool you've ever used treats a line break as the end of something, a text editor's own line count, a naive reader, all of them.
A properly quoted field breaks that assumption completely: a street address spanning two physical lines is still one single field, one single record.
Split on the line break instead of actually parsing the quotes, and you don't get an error. You get a silently wrong record count.
Ask yourself, for a second, whether a number with this many digits sitting plainly in a file could possibly come back wrong. It looks completely exact.
Nothing in the file changes. The bytes on disk never move. What changes is the choice a reader makes about how to hold that number in memory.
A parser that keeps every digit exact hands it back untouched. A parser that stores it the way most languages store a number by default hands you back a value one smaller, with no warning at all.
Open this file in a plain text editor and you will see nothing wrong with it at all. It looks like an ordinary, well formed object.
The problem lives in a few bytes before the text even starts, bytes your editor doesn't bother showing you, that exist purely to signal which encoding the file is in.
A reader that doesn't know to skip that signal treats it as the file's actual first character, and the very first thing it expects to see is already wrong.
Every single trap you just watched traces back to the same missing piece: none of these formats carries a type, or a schema, anywhere in the file itself.
A reader has to guess the structure every single time it opens one, which is exactly the guessing that broke in five different ways just now.
That's the real reason none of them is where data actually lives. They're a doorway data passes through, not a place it stays.
Five readers, each one confidently doing exactly what it was told, and each one wrong in its own way: a comma, a quote, a line break, a number, an invisible signature.
Every fix was the same shape too: stop guessing the structure, and actually parse it the way the format's own rule says to.
Underneath every one of these files is still a row of values. Whether that row is stored a row at a time or a column at a time is the very next question.
